articleTitle: On the pre-training of boys for apprenticeship as electricians
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Before I endeavour to reply specifically to the points raised by those who have been kind enough to discuss my paper on the pre-training of apprentice-electricians, I feel that I must preface my remarks by a reference to world conditions that at first sight may not appear relative to my subject, which was really a certain form of education. But it is more and more borne in upon me that the conditions to which I am about to refer are, if not wholly yet very largely, due to insufficient forms of education in the past. It will be admitted that the two outstanding features of the present conditions is the problem of international relations on the one hand and of industrial relations upon the other. The balance-of-power theory underlies both; for, in the case of international relationships, this takes the form of equality of armaments, while in industrialism it is that of collective bargaining. In both forms the underlying idea of the security of the mass was a great advance upon that having the individual, whether a nation or a person, as its origin. It is a theory of equality based upon the balancing of might against might, and it has broken down both internationally and industrially because it has all the demerits of a conflict instead of the merits of co-operation, all the hostility of opposing instead of the partnership of common interests. Patriotism and class-consciousness are both dangerous emotions when they lead to the exploitation of a part of humanity, since then they become contrary to the principle of co-operation, now essential to humanity as a whole, owing to increased interdependence in modern times. Security as a menace to the security of others is unthinkable in any Christian community.

abstract: Licensing of Wiremen. — Some discussion took place at the annual meeting of the Victorian Institute of Electrical Engineers in Melbourne regarding the licensing of wiremen. Mr. Noel Murray, a member of the Council of the Institute, desired that the municipal authorities be approached in the matter, as at present there was an enormous amount of bad work being put in. The only way to obviate this, in Mr. Murray's opinion, was to issue licenses to the wiremen in the same way as is done with engine drivers and plumbers. which would give the authorities control over the men. If a man wired a building in a faulty manner, then he should have his license suspended for six or twelve months, and this would be the means of raising the standard of work in the wiring world. A man should also be made responsible for the material used as well as for the work done. Mr. P. Rosling, the newly-elected president of the Institute, stated that the committee had considered the matter, but nothing could be done without passing au Act of Parliament. He therefore suggested that the matter should be left over until the wiremen's wages board was settled. Mr. E. H. W. Westwood said that in Wellington (N.Z.) no wireman was allowed to touch the Council's mains unless he held a license, but he believed the whole thing had proved a failure. It was eventually decided to bring the matter before the council, who would report upon it at the next meeting. — The Australian Mining Standard, March 29, 1911, p. 310.

articleTitle: A few notes on oversea wireless stations heard in Johannesburg
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The question of the successful reception of overseas high-powered transmitting stations should not be one of difficulty to the serious experimenter, and at times it is a less difficult proposition than that of receiving some of our local coast and ships' stations. The power at the hack of the larger Continental and American stations is such that with suitable coils and a valve, little difficulty, if any, should be experienced in satisfactorily reading them at any time of the day, provided, of course, that atmospheric conditions are good. Quite a number of the stations send at a very moderate rate, and the experimenter who is able to read fifteen words a minute should be able to take down such work, especially as in most eases each word is repeated. This offers a splendid opportunity to the keen worker to increase his morse-reading ability. It seems somewhat incomprehensible that anyone can derive any great enjoyment from listening to a meaningless jumble of sounds, and, furthermore, not even knowing from which part of the globe the signals emanate. At various times details of minor occurrences have been noted, which, although of only minute importance, are yet interesting to a degree to the keen observer.

articleTitle: The electrical kitchen for private houses
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is somewhat remarkable that in spite of many of the advantages which electric cooking offers, comparatively few homes, even in the larger towns, are equipped in this respect. Durban is probably the only town in this country which makes an exception, largely due to the enterprise of its City Electrical Engineer. I doubt whether even 5 per cent of all houses in most towns do all their cooking electrically, though hot plates, toasters, kettles and irons are found fairly frequently, to be used mainly in cases of emergency. Some people who tried electric cooking gave it up again on account of excessive repair bills and the inconvenience connected with the burning out of elements. This shows that there must be many defects still connected with electric cooking appliances and room for considerable improvements. With this in view I commenced a series of invstigations, not so much from the standpoint of the scientist but in close collaboration with the master of the kitchen — the housewife.

articleTitle: Balance of report of the ordinary general meeting of February 15th, 1923 domestic load building: A few suggestions upon propaganda work
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The object of this paper is to show in a simple manner some of the channels open to electric supply undertakings for securing the domestic load. As conditions differ in almost every district, the subject must be approached from a different angle in each case. In certain districts it. might be fatal to adopt a too progressive attitude, and one must therefore lead up to the point by suggestion; in others it may be found desirable to combine the development scheme, such as an educative campaign by actual demonstration, with Press and other advertisements. These methods are briefly discussed and reference is made to the value of the load to the undertaking, and the various proportions it. can take. A skeleton scheme of one year's campaign is put forward, and, in view of the decision of certain authorities to embark upon this deevlopnient, it is hoped that the remarks may be of interest. The fundamental essentials on the question of tariffs, load characteristics, hire of appliances, etc., are discussed, and a chart showing one week's demand on a housing estate, where cookers, heaters, etc., are installed, is given. The advantage of an electrically equipped household to the consumer and its appeal to women, also the assistance given by the latter in achieving the object, are referred to.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The Vice-President: There are two items down here on which members are asked to contribute their experience. I have some rather interesting information here, from Mr. Shirras, who is the Engineer to Messrs. Pyott's, Ltd. In 1917 they equipped their place electrically with some large motors, 81 h.p. They desired to instal squirrel-cage motors, and, to get over the starting torque difficulty, it was arranged to connect these to the existing two lines of shafting by means of friction clutches and to drive by chain drive. Those of you who have had any experience with flour mill drives will know that the starting torque required to start up a flour mill is something enormous, even when the mill is clear. If, however, an involuntary shutdown takes place and the whole of the milling machines and the elevators are choked with partially ground flour, then it is an extremely difficult problem to start at all. In this case the original drive was by means of a large horizontal steam engine with a multiple rope drive driving on to the two shafts, and it was decided to divide the drive up electrically between two motors, to start the motors up light, and then switch in the load by means of a friction clutch. The five years' experience of the friction clutches is rather interesting.

articleTitle: Should central station auxiliary plant be driven by electricity or steam?
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member): In the early days of electricity supply the question of the method of driving Central Station auxiliaries was not a particularly important one, and they were usually driven in the most convenient manner. Reciprocating engines were often self-contained units, the condensing auxiliaries being mechanically driven from the engine itself. The boiler draft fans were also often direct driven from a small high speed engine, or at any rate such a combination was kept as standby to a motor-driven fan.

abstract: The Vice-President: Before we pass on to the next item I have been reminded that I should have drawn your attention under “General Business” to the Electricity Bill now before Parliament. The Electricity Bill of 1922 was rather sprung upon us in South Africa. Last year the Government, through the Minister of Mines and Industries, was good enough to submit a Draft Bill to the Technical Societies, and other bodies interested, for their comments and suggestions. The Institution of Engineers and our Institute formed a Joint Committee, and we went very carefully into the clauses of the Draft Bill. Certain recommendations were made which were sent to Capetown, but the Bill was withdrawn entirely. I do not know whether our objections helped to throw the Bill out or not; but this year a new Bill was sprung upon us without notice — in fact, the Bill was down for the second reading in the House before the “Government Gazette” containing the Bill was in our hands in Johannesburg. However, owing to sending telegraphic protests to Capetown the Bill was sent to a Select Committee, which gave us an opportunity again of sending our recommendations to Capetown, The Council of your Institute formed with the Institution of Engineers a Joint Committee to again go into the new Bill. Probably some of you have studied this Bill, but it would take too long to discuss tonight the clauses in detail. From our point of view one of the bodies suggested under this new Act, viz., the Control Board, a body formed entirely of Government servants, was one clause to which we are objecting most strongly. The Joint Committee prepared their report, submitted it to their respective Councils, and Mr. Elsdon Dew and Mr. Otley are presenting it to the Select Committee, but we have not heard the result. Mr. Sankey, who went down on behalf of the Municipality of Johannesburg, may be able to tell us something to-night.

articleTitle: A description of a modern receiving equipment
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The set which we have here to-night comprises the Western Electric three-valve power amplifier and lond-speaker, which I described a month or so ago, but this evening we have in addition the Western Electric tuner and detector unit with two low frequency amplifying units attached. This set embodies the latest American practice, and is typical of high-class apparatus made in that country. The first unit contains the aerial tuming inductance, which has three tappings controlled by the switch on the upper left hand comer of the panel; the aerial series condenser, controlled by the lower left hand knob; the primary-secondary vario coupler, controlled by the knob in the top-centre of the panel; the fixed secondary inductance; the secondary parallel condenser, controlled by the lower middle knob; the valve, which can be viewed through the gauze-covered hole in the top right hand corner of the panel: the filament resistance, controlled by the knob in the lower right hand corner of the. panel, and the necessary blocking condensers, etc. The low frequency amplifying units each contain a shell type inter-valve transformer, a valve and valve holder and a filament resistance controlled by the knob in the lower part of the panel. The valve can be viewed through a gauzo-eovored hole. The various terminais on these units are symmetrically arranged so that connections can be made from one unit to another by means of straight links. The wave length range of this set is from 300 to 600 metres. This receiving set utilises Western Electric “Peanut” valves, which require only from 8 to 10 volt across the filaments, and which take only about a quarter of an ampere each, so that this equipment can be operated entirely from dry batteries. The plate potential for this type of tube when used as a detector is from 17 to 22½ volts, and when used as an amplifier from 40 to 45 volts. The telephones for use with this set are provided with a plug, and each unit contains a suitable jack, so that the phones can be plugged in immediately after the detector or after one or two stages of amplification as desired. The jacks provided do not break the filament circuit of the valves not in use, and these have to be turned out by means of the individual filament resistances which have an “off” position. The inter-valve transformers in this set are specially designed to have an impedance suited to the “peanut” type of tube. Fig. 1. shows a wiring diagram of the set. The three-valve power amplifier contains the necessary inter-valve transformers, which are of the shell type and have an impedance suited to the tubes employed, which uro in this instance Western Electric Type 216A. The filaments of these tubes are supplied from a 6-volt accumulator, and the plate potential is derived from a dry battery of from 120 to 130 volts. An additional small battery of 9 volts is used to put a negative bias on the grids of the valves. This battery is contained in the instrument. A five-point switch controlls the amount of amplification by menus of tappings till the primary of the first transformer. Fig. 2 shows the amplifier and loud-speaker. The loud-speaker itself consists of a receiver of the balanced armature type contained in the cylindrical metal base, upon which is mounted the horn of specially moulded material. Fig. 3 shows the internal arrangements of this instrument.
